title: Checkpoint signer key rotation and revocation

scientific_lineage.scientific_result: 3 passed / 13 errors in Pilot 12; 994-test suite not green
scientific_lineage.summary: The Pilot 12 fixture omitted initialization of the pre-existing convergence_reconciliation ledger. The signer child correctly attempted to derive governed reconciliation state, raised before returning the first K1 issuance, and surfaced as SIGNER_RESPONSE_LOST. The first failure is retained as experiment lineage rather than overwritten.

Only the diagnosis-authorized fixture initialization was changed. The Pilot 12 mechanism and frozen P12-01..P12-16 endpoints/expected outcomes were unchanged. Every P12 endpoint explicitly executed and passed on evaluated SHA 5ef36d6af3861ffa5ac69a21d1e4e8fe255d5f81; the complete governed-platform governor suite passed 994/994.

supported_claim: On the tested same-host Ubuntu 24.04 / Python 3.12 / SQLite / OpenSSL prototype, checkpoint-signing-key eligibility was governed by a durable platform trust registry separate from checkpoint signer, writer and verifier surfaces. K1-to-K2 and K2-to-K3 transitions advanced trust epoch and activation generation exactly once; revoked prior keys remained mathematically verifiable for historical audit but were ineligible for current trust and new issuance. Key-id/fingerprint substitution, trust-epoch rollback, stale verifier/cache reactivation, mixed-key lineage substitution and post-revocation K1 issuance were rejected. Exact replay remained idempotent, concurrent rotation versus issuance produced one authoritative outcome on the exercised path, restart preserved current trust enforcement, and models/reviewers/writers/verifiers/signers gained no production, release, merge or approval authority from trust state or signatures.
not_proven: Integrity of the trust registry against compromise of its own signing key or same-host private-key file
HSM or KMS nonextractability for registry or checkpoint-signing private keys
Protection against same-user filesystem access, debugger, ptrace, process-memory inspection, host administrator, kernel, hypervisor or physical host compromise
Secure recovery after actual compromise of the active trust-registry signing key
implementation_note: The trust-registry authority still persists its Ed25519 private key as a same-host PEM file and signs registry transitions itself. Pilot 12 therefore proves bounded transition semantics and current-use revocation behavior, not integrity after compromise of the trust-registry authority/key itself.
next_falsification_target: EXP-I Pilot 13: trust-registry root isolation and compromise containment. Remove registry private-key material from ordinary registry reader/writer surfaces, isolate trust-transition signing in a distinct authority process, bind readers to a pinned public root plus monotonic trusted-minimum trust epoch, and falsify coherent SQLite rollback/rewrite, old-valid-registry replay, forged/replaced registry roots, post-compromise stale-key reactivation, signer/registry collusion attempts, authority-process outage, restart, and clean K3-to-K4 liveness without granting models, reviewers, checkpoint signers or registry readers trust-mutation authority.
